props.title: Cleopatra

sections.content: Theda Bara's portrayal in Cleopatra (1917) marks a pivotal moment in early Hollywood's fascination with ancient Egypt and female sexuality. This lavish Fox Film Corporation production, now largely lost except for brief fragments, showcased unprecedented production values for its time, with elaborate sets and reportedly 50 different costumes for Bara alone. The film followed the success of Intolerance (1916) in proving that American cinema could handle epic historical subjects with sophistication, paving the way for later spectacles like The Ten Commandments (1923).

sections.content: The 1917 Cleopatra established many visual tropes that would define Hollywood's Egypt for decades - the revealing costumes, ornate headpieces, and exotic set design. Director J. Gordon Edwards created what was then the most expensive film production to date, though its controversial marketing campaign focusing on Bara's "vampire" persona and revealing costumes led to censorship in several cities. The film's approach to spectacle directly influenced later Egyptian-themed epics like The Egyptian (1954) and Land of the Pharaohs (1955).

Theda Bara's performance style in Cleopatra exemplified the transition from exaggerated theatrical gestures to a more naturalistic screen presence. While still broad by modern standards, her portrayal helped bridge the gap between stage and screen acting techniques, influencing stars like Gloria Swanson in Male and Female (1919) and Betty Blythe in The Queen of Sheba (1921). sections.content: The loss of most of Cleopatra represents a broader tragedy of silent film preservation. Like many films of its era, including the original Queen of Sheba (1921) and Salomé (1918), it fell victim to vault fires and nitrate film decomposition. The surviving fragments, mostly publicity stills and brief clips, hint at the film's groundbreaking visual effects and set design that would influence historical epics for generations.
